turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): in you come. i'll get a blood pressure while doctor reeves argues with the computer. my sister's little one was coughing all night so i'm a bit slow, ignore me.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): oh, um, thanks. i've been a wreck about this all week, sorry.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): one thirty two over eighty four, pulse seventy eight. that's fine. arm down.
[SEG0004] person_3 (DOCTOR): morning. sorry, the screen's frozen again. what's brought you in?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): my lower back. the pain shoots down my left leg, three weeks now, and i can't stop thinking it's something awful.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): left leg, did you say? once more, i was clicking.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): yes, left. it starts low in the back and shoots down the back of the thigh into the calf. three weeks. it's worse when i sit.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): right. sitting. what do you do all day?

[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): desk job, accounts, so i'm sat for hours. umm, a colleague told me to do those lie-on-your-front stretches and i've been having a go in the evenings. not sure i'm doing them right. does that make the nerve worse?
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): we'll come to the stretches. are you taking anything for the pain?

[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): neurofen, the orange capsules. and sorry, random, but my dad's diabetic, he's on metforman for it, and he keeps telling me to mention that, that's his though. i haven't got diabetes, should i be worried i will?
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): no, that's his tablet, not yours. what dose of nurofen? the screen jumped, say it again.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): uh, 400 milligrams, three times a day, with food. for about a fortnight.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): any problems passing water, or with your bowels? numbness between the legs, the saddle area?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): no. waterworks are fine, bowels are fine, no numbness there. i checked because i read something and panicked.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): and the leg, weakness, or pins and needles?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): tingling in the left foot, comes and goes. i don't think the leg's weak, i can walk on it, i'm just frightened it'll give.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): shoes off, lie back. straight leg raise on the left, stop there, that's about forty degrees and it sets the pain off. right leg lifts fine, no pain.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): ow, yep, that's exactly it. is forty degrees terrible? does that mean i've slipped a disc? will i need an operation?
[SEG0020] person_1 (NURSE): i'll jot forty degrees. my own back went after my second, totally separate, the midwife just told me to walk.

[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): what's happening is the disc is irritating the nerve as it leaves the lower spine, and that nerve runs down the leg, so the pain shoots. that fits the straight leg raise. it does not mean an operation, and it isn't anything nasty.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): so is it definitely a disc? should i have a scan, my colleague said push for an mri. and can i still drive? i drive in every day and i'm really anxious about the pedal.

[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): i'm not calling it definite, it's my working impression. no scan today. if it hasn't settled with physio in six weeks we'll think about an mri. driving is alright if you can do an emergency stop without the pain stopping you.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): and those stretches, do i carry on? what if i make it worse? sorry, too many questions.

[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): little and often, on your front, stop if it sharpens the leg pain. don't force it. i'm referring you to physiotherapy, that'll be booked. and i'll see you back here in six weeks.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): the neurofen though. 400 three times, is that too much? my stomach's been a bit queasy after them, not pain, just queasy. should i stop tonight?
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): sorry, queasy, say that again?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): yeah, a bit sick-feeling after the orange capsules. not every dose. maybe half of them.

[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): keep the nurofen at 400 milligrams three times a day with food for now. if the queasiness gets properly worse, stop it and use paracetamol instead, two 500 milligram tablets up to four times a day. don't add another anti-inflammatory on top.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): and if the tingling spreads, or i can't wee, i don't wait six weeks, do i? i keep imagining the worst.

[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): if you can't pass water, or you lose bowel control, or the numbness is spreading, that's a and e the same day, don't wait for me. otherwise six weeks. nurse will sort the physio and the appointment.
[SEG0032] person_1 (NURSE): i'll book the six weeks and send the physio referral before you go. try not to sit googling all evening. my sister did that with her own knee and it did her no favours.

spec.situation: Person with low back pain shooting down one leg for three weeks, worse sitting; takes ibuprofen; a colleague's advice on exercises; doctor examines straight-leg raise and plans physio, no scan yet.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

features: third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

omissions.text: Current ibuprofen/Neurofen was specifically being taken with food.
Patient denied pain with right straight leg raise: right leg lifts fine, no pain.
Doctor reassured that this does not mean an operation and is not anything nasty.
Doctor explicitly said he was not calling it definite and that disc irritation was only a working impression.
Physio referral would be booked by the nurse, and the six-week follow-up appointment would also be booked by the nurse before the patient leaves.
